ATOMIC MASS · %1$s
ELEMENT COLLECTION / %1$03d
Preview · all 118 elements available · artistic motifs
Lilac flame
Potassium salts colour the flame lilac in a flame test.
Melting metal
Gallium melts at about 29.8 °C. This sample softens into a metallic pool.
Silver coinage
Coins evoke historical silver currency, often alloyed with copper.
Food tin
Tinplate is steel sheet coated with a thin layer of tin.
Platinum jewellery
The setting evokes platinum jewellery alloys. The stone represents a diamond, not platinum.
Golden bullion
Bullion bars illustrate the characteristic metallic colour of gold.
Infrared lens
Germanium transmits infrared radiation and is used in infrared optics. The rays use false colours; they are invisible to the eye.
Grey arsenic is a brittle solid with a metallic lustre. The plates and reflections are stylised; the material does not emit light.
Selenium light meter
Selenium is sensitive to light. Selenium cells were used in photographic exposure meters; the needle illustrates the measurement of illumination.
Bromine under glass
At room temperature, bromine is a volatile reddish-brown liquid. The sealed ampoule shows liquid and vapour, not flames.
Photographic flash
Krypton is used in some flash lamps for high-speed photography. The glow illustrates an electrical discharge, not the colour of the unexcited gas.
Rubidium clock
Some atomic clocks use a rubidium vapour cell as a frequency reference. The dial symbolises timekeeping; motion is slowed down and schematic.
Red signal flare
Strontium salts give signal flares their red colour. The illustration depicts this use of compounds, not the pure metal.
YAG laser crystal
Yttrium aluminium garnet (YAG), doped with active ions, is used as a laser medium. The coloured beam is schematic; the crystal is not metallic yttrium.
Zirconia blade
Zirconia, zirconium dioxide, is used to make very hard ceramic blades. The white blade represents this oxide, not the metal.
Superconducting coil
Niobium-containing alloys are used in superconducting magnets at very low temperatures. The glowing lines symbolise the normally invisible magnetic field.
Alloy steel drill bit
Molybdenum is used in tool alloys, including drill bits. The drawing evokes wear-resistant alloy steel, not a drill made of pure molybdenum.
Cyclotron and irradiated target
Technetium was identified in 1937 in molybdenum irradiated by a cyclotron. This stylised cutaway evokes that research; it is neither a visible sample nor an exact reconstruction.
Electrical contacts
Ruthenium is used in wear-resistant alloys for electrical contacts. The drawing enlarges the contacts; the entire switch is not made of ruthenium.
Catalytic converter cutaway
Rhodium catalyses the reduction of nitrogen oxides in exhaust gases. The honeycomb represents the support carrying the catalytic coating; the coloured flows are symbolic.
Hydrogen membrane
Hydrogen diffuses through heated palladium, allowing it to be purified. The illustration simplifies molecular dissociation, atomic passage and recombination; this is not a sieve with holes.
Pigment palette
Cadmium compounds have been used in yellow, orange and red pigments. The palette evokes this historical use; the metal is silvery and these compounds pose toxicity risks.
Conductive touch glass
Transparent, conductive indium tin oxide (ITO) is used in touchscreens. The offset layer and ripples make its role visible; the display is not made of pure indium.
Tree, roots and coal seam
Wood is built from carbon taken from the air. Plants buried for millions of years slowly turned into coal: the fern imprint is a fossil.
Solfatara
Around volcanic vents (fumaroles), native sulfur crystallises as yellow crusts and crystals.
Forge trip hammer
Cams turned by a water wheel lifted a heavy hammer that forged red-hot iron bars.
Electric motor
After silver, copper is the best conductor of electricity: it fills cables, the windings of every motor, and the pipes that carry water through the house.
The Sun, a star of hydrogen
About three quarters of the Sun\'s mass is hydrogen. In its core, hydrogen nuclei fuse into helium. The red prominences at its edge glow with the light of hydrogen.
Balloon release
Helium is about seven times less dense than air, so a balloon filled with it rises. Unlike hydrogen, it does not burn.
Panning for gold
Gold is about nineteen times denser than water. When a prospector swirls sand in a pan, the light grains wash away and the gold stays at the bottom, as flakes or sometimes a nugget.
Breathing
With every breath the lungs fill with air, about one fifth of which is oxygen. In the tiny air sacs at the end of the bronchi, oxygen passes into the blood, which the heart pumps to the whole body.
Neon sign
Neon glows red-orange when an electric current passes through it. The other colours of neon signs come from other gases or from coloured coatings on the glass.
Fireworks
Magnesium burns with a dazzling white light. Ground to a fine powder in fireworks, it gives the brilliant white sparks and the crackling stars.
Wheat field
Nitrogen makes up almost four fifths of the air, yet plants can only draw it from the soil. Fertilisers bring it to them: without nitrogen, no wheat, and no bread.
Lithium-ion battery
Lithium is the lightest of all metals. In a battery, its ions cross from one electrode to the other: into the graphite while charging, back out while the phone or the car draws power.
Microchip
Silicon is drawn from sand. Purified and sliced into wafers, it carries billions of tiny switches on a chip no bigger than a fingernail, the heart of every computer and phone.
Tooth and toothpaste
The fluoride in toothpaste settles into the enamel, the hardest tissue in the body, and makes it tougher against the acids that cause cavities.
Salt marsh
Table salt is sodium chloride. In the salt marshes, sun and wind evaporate the sea water and the salt crystallises; the salt worker rakes it up and piles it in white mounds.
Swimming pool
A small dose of chlorine kills the germs in the water: it keeps swimming pools clear, and it also makes our tap water safe to drink.
Light bulb
The tungsten filament glows white hot. In air it would burn out at once, so the bulb is filled with argon, a gas that reacts with nothing.
Bones of the hand
Calcium is what makes bones hard: the skeleton holds almost all of the body’s calcium. Milk, cheese and green vegetables bring it to us.
Thermometer
Mercury is the only metal that is liquid at room temperature. It expands as it warms, which is why it rose in the tube of old thermometers. Its vapour is toxic.
Striking a match
The striking strip on the box holds red phosphorus. Rubbing the match head on it turns a pinch of it into white phosphorus, which catches fire at once and lights the head.
Nuclear power plant
In the reactor, uranium nuclei split and release heat. It boils water whose steam drives the turbines; what rises from the great towers is only water vapour.
Silverware by candlelight
Silver reflects light better than any other metal: that is why it was used for mirrors, cutlery and candlesticks. It darkens in air and must be polished.
Banana tree
Potassium keeps the nerves and muscles working, the heart included. The banana is the best-known fruit that is rich in it.
Space telescope
Light, and it keeps its shape in the deep cold of space: beryllium makes the eighteen mirror segments of the James Webb telescope, coated with a thin film of gold.
Glass kettle
A little boron in glass, and it takes the flame without cracking: it is the glass of see-through kettles and of dishes that go in the oven.
Soda can
Light, and it never rusts: aluminium makes drink cans, and it can be recycled again and again without losing anything.
Racing bike
A pinch of scandium in aluminium makes the metal stiffer and lighter: just right for racing bike frames.
Airliner
As strong as steel but almost half as heavy, and it never rusts: titanium goes into the landing gear, the engines and the wing joints of airliners.
Car suspension spring
A little vanadium makes steel hard and springy: it goes into car springs, which take every bump without ever losing their shape, and into the best tools.
Chrome tap
A layer of chromium thinner than a hair makes metal shine like a mirror and keeps it from ever rusting: taps, handlebars and bumpers.
Flashlight
Inside every alkaline battery there is manganese dioxide: it is the black powder that, together with zinc, gives the current to the flashlight.
Blue and white vase
Painted on raw porcelain, cobalt oxide turns in the kiln into a deep blue that never fades: the blue of china vases and plates.
Spinning coin
Hard, shiny and hard-wearing, nickel goes into coins: the silver-coloured part of 1 and 2 euro coins contains it.
Paris rooftops
Zinc does not rust: it weathers to a soft blue-grey and lasts a hundred years. Most of the roofs of Paris are covered with it.
Melting spoon
Gallium melts at 30 °C, the warmth of a hand: a gallium spoon melts in hot tea and sinks to the bottom in drops of liquid metal.
Thermal camera
Germanium lets through the infrared that glass stops: thermal camera lenses are made of it, to see in the dark the warmth of animals and houses.
Satellite
Combined with gallium, arsenic makes the most efficient solar cells: they power satellites and the rovers on Mars.
Photocopier
Selenium only conducts electricity when light falls on it: the drums of the first photocopiers were coated with it, and the light drew the page on them.
Hot tub in the snow
Bromine keeps the water of hot tubs clean: unlike chlorine, it still works well in hot water.
Laser show
Krypton lasers long painted the red beams of laser shows; krypton also lights airport runways.
GPS on the trail
GPS satellites carry rubidium atomic clocks: their extremely precise time is what lets a phone work out where it is.
Red distress flare
Strontium salts give their bright red to distress flares and fireworks.
Laser cutter
Yttrium aluminium garnet, the “YAG” crystal, is the heart of the lasers that cut through steel; it also turns the light of white LEDs white.
Zircon ring
Zirconia, an oxide of zirconium cut like a diamond, sparkles and throws even more rainbow fire than a diamond does.
MRI scanner
The great magnet of an MRI scanner is a superconducting coil of niobium-titanium wire, cooled with liquid helium.
Drill press
A few percent of molybdenum makes the “high-speed steel” of drill bits: it stays hard even when cutting heats it red.
Bone scan
Technetium-99m is the isotope most used in hospitals: once injected it settles on the bones, and a camera counts one by one the rays it gives off.
Hard drive
A layer of ruthenium just three atoms thick, slipped into the platters of hard drives, let them hold far more data.
Explain the picture

The Sun seen through a telescope. The disc darkens toward its edge; the fine grains are bubbles of burning gas, and the dark spots are sunspots drifting past as it turns. The red flames on the rim are prominences, jets of hydrogen bigger than the Earth.
A bunch of helium balloons held above the rooftops of a town. They tug at their strings and jostle each other, while two runaways rise in the distance.

A cylindrical battery cut open: inside, a long roll of thin sheets. The magnifying glass shows what happens there: while charging, the lithium ions (the small balls) cross the wall in the middle and slip between the layers of graphite; while discharging, they go back. The gauge follows their trip.

The James Webb space telescope, in the dark of space. Its great golden honeycomb mirror stands on the sunshield, five stacked silver sails that keep the Sun\'s heat away. A gleam slides across the gold, and a distant galaxy slowly turns.
A glass kettle on the blue flame of a gas stove. The water boils hard and steam rushes out of the spout, yet the glass does not crack.
An oak tree, with the ground cut open beneath it: first its roots, then deeper down a black seam of coal. In the coal lies the print of a fern, a plant from very long ago that turned into coal.
A field of ripe wheat. The wind sweeps across it in pale waves, and the tall ears in front bow as it reaches them.

The chest drawn as in an anatomy book: the windpipe and its rings, the two lungs, the bronchi branching like a tree, and the heart nestled against the left lung. The lungs fill and empty, air comes in and out, the heart beats.

A tooth cut in half: the white enamel outside, the dentine beneath it, the pink pulp in the middle with its blood vessels, then the gum and the bone. The brush scrubs, the toothpaste foams, and the small dots that sink in are fluoride ions settling into the enamel to harden it.
A café sign at night, in the rain: a cup drawn with glass tubes full of neon. The tubes light up one after another, one of them flickers, and the glow is reflected on the wet cobblestones.

A salt marsh in the sun: shallow pools of seawater. With his long rake, the salt worker pulls in the salt that has crystallised and piles it into white heaps. In the distance a windmill turns and gulls fly by.
Fireworks over a river at night. The rockets are launched from a barge, burst into big white spheres, then their stars crackle before fading out; the water mirrors every flash.

A seaside terrace: an open can and a glass full of ice cubes on the table. Bubbles rise in the glass, a drop of condensation runs down the can, a wasp circles around, and the edge of the parasol ripples in the wind.

A chip on its circuit board, with its case open. In the middle sits the silicon wafer and its computing cores, linked by fine gold wires; signals run along the copper tracks and through the pins, and the cores light up as they compute.
A hand strikes a match on the side of the box. The match bursts into flame, burns and blackens, then it is shaken and goes out in a wisp of smoke.
The crater of a sleeping volcano that still smokes. The fumes rise from cracks in the ground and leave yellow crusts behind: that is sulfur. The plume rises and drifts; in front lie sulfur crystals.
A swimming pool whose water is so clear that you can see the tiles on the bottom, under a net of dancing light. A swimmer does lengths between the lane ropes.
An old-fashioned light bulb switching on. The thin wire in the middle, the filament, goes from red to white as it heats up, the room brightens, and a moth comes to circle around it.
A banana plant on a plantation. Its large leaves, torn by the wind, sway; the bunch of bananas hangs under a big purple flower bud, and a blue butterfly flutters by.

The skeleton of a hand and wrist, seen from the back as in an anatomy book. The fingers spread like a fan and close again, and a wave bends them one after another: you can see each small bone turn on the next.
A cyclist speeds along a country road. The wheels spin, the legs pedal, and the posts, trees and clouds slide past, each at its own speed: the farther away they are, the slower they go by.
An airliner above a sea of clouds. The clouds slide by below, the long white trails behind the engines stretch out, and the navigation lights blink.

An old car on the road. Above the wheel, the bodywork is drawn see-through, like a mechanic\'s diagram: at every bump the wheel jumps, the spring squeezes then stretches out again, and the car body stays steady.
A chrome tap over a washbasin. The water runs, splashes and makes rings around the drain, while a gleam of light slides along the mirror-bright metal.

An attic in the dark. The beam of a flashlight sweeps the room and brings out a trunk, a globe, a painting, and a cat whose eyes light up; dust dances in the light. The flashlight runs on batteries, and that is where the manganese is.

A forge from the old days. A turning shaft with bumps on it, the cams, lifts the handle of a huge hammer, which falls back onto the red-hot iron bar and sends sparks flying. Horseshoes hang on the wall; on the left are the hearth and its hood.
A large white porcelain vase painted in blue, slowly turning on its stand. As it turns, its patterns pass before us: banana leaves at the neck, peonies on the belly, lotus flowers at the foot.

A two-colour coin, like a 1 or 2 euro coin, spinning on its edge in the middle of a table, between a piggy bank and a stack of coins. Its two faces show in turn, and its ridged edge appears when it turns side-on.

An electrician\'s workbench. In the middle, an open motor: you can see the coils of copper wire wound around its poles. When the lever switch is closed, the current flows, the motor speeds up and its brushes crackle; when it is opened, a spark flies and the motor slows down. On the wall, copper pipes.
The rooftops of Paris at dusk. In front, a blue-grey zinc roof with its chimney and a lit dormer window; behind it, more roofs, a dome, and the sparkling Eiffel Tower.
A glass cup of hot tea. A gallium spoon dips into it and melts from the tip: drops of liquid metal fall to the bottom. It comes out shorter, goes away, and a new spoon comes down.

A garden at night, almost black, and in front of it the screen of a thermal camera showing the same garden by its heat: the passing fox glows white and yellow, the heated window turns red, and the cold sky stays dark.
A satellite above the Earth, which turns slowly below it. Its body is wrapped in gold foil, and its two big blue wings are solar panels: they swivel to follow the Sun and flash when they face it.
A photocopier with its lid open. A bar of light passes under the glass to read the sheet, comes back, and the copy slides out of the machine into the tray.
A winter night in the mountains: a wooden hot tub on the terrace of a chalet. The lit water bubbles, steam rises, snow falls.
A smoky concert hall. Red and green laser beams fan out and sweep through the haze above the jumping crowd, and the hanging spotlights change colour.
At dusk, a hiker on a ridge looks at the map on his phone. GPS satellites pass in the sky, their signals come down in waves to the phone, and the blue dot of his position pulses on the map.
At night at sea, a sailboat fires a distress flare. It climbs, opens under a small parachute, then drifts slowly down, lighting the sea in red; when it goes out, another one is fired.
A laser cutting machine. The cutting head runs along its gantry and traces a star in a steel sheet: the line glows red behind it for a moment, then turns black, and sparks shoot out under the beam.
A ring in its velvet box, under a turning light. The stone is cubic zirconia: its facets light up one after another and throw out rainbow-coloured sparkles.

An MRI scanner seen from the front: the big white machine with its round tunnel. The patient lies on the table, feet in socks toward us, and the table slides him into the tunnel. During the scan, the tunnel flashes blue and the small screen at the top right draws an image of his head, line by line. Then the table brings him back out.
A drill press in a workshop. The bit spins and bores into a steel block held in a vice; now and then it lifts out to clear the hole, and the long spiral chip breaks off and falls.

A hospital computer screen in a dark room. The patient\'s skeleton appears dot by dot, front and back: each dot is a ray coming from his bones. Once the image is complete, it fades away for the next scan.

A hard drive opened on a workbench. The mirror-bright disc spins very fast; the read arm, with its tiny head at the tip, jumps from track to track and bounces slightly at each stop. The green light blinks whenever it moves.

Under a moving car, the catalytic converter is cut open so you can see inside. The dirty engine gases come in from the left (the small black, blue and red molecules), pass through the hot orange honeycomb, and come out on the right turned into harmless gases: nitrogen, carbon dioxide and water vapour.
A table by candlelight: a candlestick, a teapot and silver cutlery. The flames flicker and their reflections dance on the metal.

A gold prospector kneels by a mountain river and swirls his pan, a kind of wide shallow dish. The water carries the sand away, and the nugget, much heavier, stays at the bottom and shines. Behind him are his tent and his campfire.
A mercury thermometer by a window. When the sun comes out of the clouds, the silver column rises; when a cloud passes, it falls again. In the small dish, beads of mercury tremble.
A nuclear power plant by a river. The big towers release nothing but water vapour: their white plumes rise and drift, the lights at the top of the towers blink, and the river flows.
Hydrogen sponge
Palladium soaks up hydrogen like a sponge: it can absorb up to nine hundred times its own volume of the gas. Since hydrogen alone can pass through it, palladium is also used to purify it.

A tank of water with an electric current running through it from a power supply. On the left, the platinum wire gives off bubbles of oxygen. On the right, the palladium strip should give off hydrogen bubbles, but it swallows the hydrogen instead: the small dots rush toward it and vanish inside, and the strip swells and bends. Once full, it starts to bubble too. When the current is switched off, the hydrogen fizzes back out and the strip straightens.
Cadmium yellow

Cadmium sulfide gives a bright yellow, and adding selenium turns it orange, then red: these are the cadmium yellows and reds in artists\' paint tubes. Cadmium is toxic, so these paints are handled with care.

A painter, seen from behind, paints a sunflower field at sunset, holding the palette in the left hand. Behind the canvas, the real landscape is engraved in muted colours; on the canvas, the same landscape blazes in cadmium yellow, orange and red. Each fresh stroke shines for a moment, then dries and blends into the painting.
Touchscreen
Every touchscreen hides a transparent layer of indium tin oxide on its glass: it conducts electricity while letting the light through, and it is this invisible grid that feels the finger.

A phone lying on a desk, seen from above. A finger taps one icon after another; at each touch, the grid of transparent wires hidden under the glass lights up for a moment, with the row and the column that cross under the finger glowing brighter than the rest. That is how the screen knows where it was touched.
Soldering
Solder wire is almost entirely tin: it melts at around 220 °C and joins electronic components to their copper tracks. It is the main use of tin.

A circuit board moves forward one notch after each joint. The hot iron comes down on a pin, the tin wire arrives and melts into a small shiny drop that fixes it to the copper; a wisp of smoke rises and the red spool unwinds a little. The pins on the left are already soldered, those on the right are waiting their turn.
Stibnite crystals
Stibnite, an antimony sulfide, grows in long steel-grey needles: it is the main ore of antimony. The metal is mostly used to make plastics and fabrics hard to set on fire.
A spray of stibnite crystals in a dim museum, slowly turning on its stand under a spotlight. Each steel needle lights up as it turns to face the light, and dust floats in the beam.
Solar farm
A layer of cadmium telluride, thinner than a hair, turns sunlight into electricity in thin, cheap solar panels laid out by the thousands in large solar farms.

Rows of solar panels stretch toward the horizon in the desert. The sun crosses the sky and the rows turn to follow it, from east to west. At nightfall they return flat under the stars, then turn back east for the dawn.
Violet vapour
When heated, the almost black crystals of iodine turn straight into a deep violet vapour without melting. On a cold surface, the vapour turns back into crystals.

Under a laboratory fume hood, a beaker of iodine crystals warms on a hot plate. The violet vapour swirls up to the flask full of ice set on top, and on its cold bottom it turns back into fine sparkling flakes.
Xenon headlights
In xenon headlights, an electric arc crosses a tiny bubble of xenon and gives off a bluish white light, far stronger than an ordinary bulb.

A car drives along a country road at night. Its headlight beam, cut sharply at the top with a blue edge, lights the road ahead. The roadside posts, the trees and a bend sign leap out of the dark as they enter the beam, then sink back into the shadow behind.
Caesium fountain clock
The second is defined by caesium: it is the time taken by 9,192,631,770 oscillations of its atoms. Caesium atomic clocks keep the world\'s official time.

An atomic fountain clock, drawn cut open. At the bottom, red lasers cool a small cloud of caesium atoms until it almost stops moving; the cloud is thrown upward, crosses the cavity where microwaves probe it, falls back, and its glow is measured on return. On the wall, the clock ticks the seconds that caesium defines.
Barium X-ray

Barium sulfate stops X-rays. Swallowed as a white drink, it outlines the oesophagus and the stomach on the X-ray image, where they would otherwise be invisible. It is harmless because it does not dissolve in the body.

A live X-ray of the chest and belly: the ribs, the spine and the beating edge of the heart. The patient swallows the white barium drink: it slides down the oesophagus and fills the stomach under a dark air bubble. Waves squeeze the stomach and push the barium into the intestine.
Camera lens
Lanthanum oxide gives glass a strong power to bend light while keeping colours sharp. It goes into camera lenses, which can then be smaller and lighter.

Looking straight into the lens of a camera. Deep inside, the blades of the iris close and open to let in less or more light. The focus ring turns back and forth, coloured reflections glide over the glass and the red self-timer light blinks.
Lighter flint
The flint of a lighter is mostly cerium mixed with iron. Scraped by the steel wheel, it sheds tiny shavings that catch fire in the air on their own: those are the sparks that light the gas.

A thumb rolls the toothed wheel of a lighter and comes to rest on the gas button. The wheel scrapes the cerium flint hidden below it: a shower of sparks flies toward the gas, which catches fire. In the clear body, the liquid gas bubbles as it escapes. When the thumb lets go, the flame goes out.
Glassblower\'s glasses
Hot glass gives off a dazzling yellow light that hides the work. Glassblowers wear glasses tinted with praseodymium and neodymium, which absorb exactly that yellow and let everything else through.

A glassblower turns a glass rod in the blue flame of a torch; its tip melts into a glowing drop. Around it, hot glass throws a yellow glare that drowns everything. The lenses of the safety glasses sway in front of us: through them the glare disappears and the molten glass shows clearly.
Neodymium magnet

Magnets made of neodymium, iron and boron are the strongest permanent magnets: a small one can hold a thousand times its own weight. They hide in earphones, phones, electric car motors and wind turbines.

Seen from above, a neodymium magnet turns slowly on a sheet of paper, with a paper clip stuck to each end. Around it, iron filings line up along the invisible lines of its field, thickest near the ends, and the needles of the four compasses turn to follow it.
Particle accelerator

In an accelerator hall, bunches of ions race around a ring of magnets: the blue ones bend their path, the red ones keep the beam narrow. A bunch is sent to the target. In the magnifier, an ion hits a heavy nucleus and merges with it: the new nucleus shakes, throws off two neutrons, then soon falls apart, spitting out alpha particles.
Research reactor

Looking down into the pool of a research reactor. The water glows blue around the core, lit by particles moving faster than light can travel in water. The control rods slide up and down to steer the reaction, and a small capsule is lowered into the core, left there, then pulled back up glowing: inside, neutrons have turned its contents into other elements.
Geiger counter

The probe of a Geiger counter moves over a block of ore. The closer it gets, the faster the counter crackles: each flash of the red light is a particle from the rock passing through the probe, and the needle rises with the count.
Open-pit mine

An open-pit mine dug in steps. Loaded dump trucks climb the track out of the pit in their dust, while an excavator digs at the bottom. The ore holds the metal mixed with many others: it still has to be separated, which is long and difficult.
This element does not exist in nature. It is made one atom at a time by firing a beam of ions at a target in an accelerator, and it falls apart again within moments.
Astatine is the rarest natural element: at any moment, there is less than a gram of it in the whole Earth\'s crust. It is made in cyclotrons, a few atoms at a time, to treat some cancers.
Francium is so unstable that no one has ever seen a visible piece of it: half of it vanishes in 22 minutes. It is made in accelerators a few hundred thousand atoms at a time, to study them.
Thallium-201, made in cyclotrons, is injected to make the heart muscle visible on a medical scan. The metal itself is soft like lead and very toxic.
Promethium has no stable form: almost all of it is made in nuclear reactors. Its faint radioactivity powers tiny long-lasting batteries and some thickness gauges.
Hafnium swallows neutrons like a sponge. Its control rods slide into a reactor\'s core to slow down or stop the chain reaction, especially in nuclear submarines.
Polonium is extremely radioactive: a single gram heats itself to over 500 °C. It is made in reactors and used in antistatic brushes that clean dust off lenses.
Neptunium is made in nuclear reactors, where uranium catches neutrons. It is used to make plutonium-238, the fuel of the nuclear batteries of space probes.
Curium is made in reactors from plutonium. Its strong radioactivity is used in instruments on Mars rovers to find out what rocks are made of.
Berkelium is made in tiny amounts in a few research reactors: barely a gram in total so far. It is used as a target to create even heavier elements.
Californium gives off a stream of neutrons on its own. A few micrograms are enough to start up a nuclear reactor or to search for oil underground.
Fermium is the heaviest element that can be made in a reactor, by piling neutrons onto lighter atoms. Only invisible traces of it have ever been made.
Radon is a radioactive gas that seeps out of granite and soils. It can build up in poorly aired cellars, which is why it is measured in houses.
Radium is so radioactive that it glows faintly and stays warmer than its surroundings. It is found in traces in uranium ores.
Actinium glows blue in the dark from its own radioactivity. Tiny amounts are now used to destroy cancer cells from the inside.
Protactinium is one of the rarest natural elements: a few grams hide in many tonnes of uranium ore, where it slowly forms.
Holmium has the strongest magnetism of all elements: it concentrates the field of the most powerful magnets. Its laser breaks up kidney stones.
Thulium is one of the rarest rare earths. It powers small portable X-ray devices and some medical lasers.
Ytterbium atoms tick in some of the most precise clocks ever built, which would not drift by a second in the age of the Universe. It also powers lasers that cut metal.
Lutetium is the last and the densest of the rare earths. Its crystals catch the flashes of light in hospital PET scanners, and it is used to treat some cancers.
Tantalum is mined from an ore called coltan. Tiny tantalum capacitors store electricity in nearly every phone and computer, and it is so harmless to the body that it is used in implants.
Guitar pickup
Samarium-cobalt magnets keep their strength even when hot. They sit under the strings of electric guitars, in pickups that turn each vibration of a string into an electric signal.

Close-up on an electric guitar in front of its amplifier. A pick strums the six strings down, then up. Each string vibrates above a magnetic pole of the pickup, and the sound comes out of the amplifier in waves before fading.
Banknote under UV light
Euro banknotes hide inks and fibres that only light up under ultraviolet light, to stop forgers. The red glow comes from europium.
A banknote lies on a counter in the dark. An ultraviolet lamp slides above it on its rail. Under its violet spot, hidden things appear: red, green and blue fibres, and a circle of stars glowing red.
MRI contrast
Injected into the blood, gadolinium makes vessels and some diseased tissues shine on MRI images. Hospitals use it for millions of scans every year.

The screen of an MRI scanner. On the right, the brain seen slice by slice: the scanner moves up and down through the head, and the line on the profile on the left shows where. Then the syringe pushes the gadolinium in, and the blood vessels light up bright white in every slice.
Fluorescent tube
Inside a fluorescent tube, a powder coats the glass and turns invisible ultraviolet light into visible light. Its green comes from terbium, the same green as in many screens.

In a dark garage, the tube on the ceiling hesitates and flickers, then lights up and reveals the pegboard of tools and the workbench. In the magnifier, the vapour inside the tube throws invisible ultraviolet rays onto the powder lining the glass, and each grain gives them back as green, red or blue light.
Offshore wind turbine
A little dysprosium keeps strong magnets working when they get hot. It is found in the generators of large wind turbines and in the motors of electric cars.

Wind turbines turn out at sea. On the nearest one, a cut-away shows the generator: a ring of magnets, north and south in turn, spins with the blades past fixed coils, which light up as each magnet passes. The current runs down the mast to the cable under the sea.
Undersea cable
The internet crosses the oceans as flashes of light in glass fibres. Every eighty kilometres or so, a stretch of fibre doped with erbium gives the fading flashes their strength back.

On the sea floor, an internet cable is shown open along its length. Flashes of light race through its glass fibres and grow fainter as they travel. In the repeater in the middle, a coil of erbium fibre glows pink: the flashes come out of it bright again. Fish swim past and seaweed sways.
Light bulb filament
Tungsten has the highest melting point of all metals. Heated to nearly 3,000 °C, the coiled wire of a light bulb glows white without melting.

A light bulb seen up close, with its coiled tungsten wire. The current rises: the filament turns dark red, then orange, yellow and finally white, and its warm light fills the room. Then it fades and goes out again.
Jet engine
The turbine blades of a jet engine sit in gases hotter than their own melting point. The rhenium in their alloy keeps them from slowly bending out of shape.

A jet engine cut in half on its stand. The fan and the compressors spin; air rushes in and is squeezed, burns in the combustion chamber, passes through the glowing red turbine blades and leaves as a scorching jet. Some of the air goes around the core without burning.
Fountain pen
Osmium is the densest of all elements and one of the hardest. A tiny bead of its alloy caps the tip of good pen nibs, which glide over paper for years without wearing out.
A fountain pen writes a line of blue loops on lined paper, lifts, and the sheet moves up a line before it starts again. In the magnifier, the tip of the nib with its small grey bead of osmium.
Spark plug
The centre electrode of the best spark plugs is made of iridium, one of the hardest metals to wear down. Millions of sparks barely erode it.

A car engine cylinder cut open. The intake valve lets the fuel mixture in, the piston squeezes it, and the spark plug fires: the flame spreads and pushes the piston down. Then the exhaust valve lets the burnt gases out, while the crankshaft keeps turning.
Hydrogen fuel cell

On a thin layer of platinum grains, hydrogen splits into protons and electrons. A fuel cell turns this into electricity, and gives off nothing but water. Platinum also cleans car exhaust in catalytic converters.

A fuel cell seen in cross-section. On the left, hydrogen molecules arrive and break apart on the grey platinum layer. Their protons (red) cross the yellow membrane, while their electrons (blue) go round through the wire and light the bulb. On the right, they meet oxygen and form drops of water, which drip out.
Fishing sinker
Lead is heavy, soft and easy to melt: it long weighed down fishing lines. Because it is toxic, it is being replaced, but most lead still goes into car batteries.

A float lands on a lake. The lead sinker drags the hook and its worm down to the bottom, leaving a trail of bubbles. A perch comes closer and nibbles, and the float dips twice. Then the line is pulled up at once and the fish darts away.
Bismuth crystal
When it cools slowly, bismuth grows in hollow, stepped squares. A very thin layer of oxide covers it and, like a soap bubble, shows every colour depending on its thickness.

A bismuth crystal turns slowly on black velvet under a spotlight. It is made of hollow square steps going down toward the centre, and each step changes colour as it turns: gold, pink, violet, blue, green. A glint runs along its corners.
Gas lantern
The mantle of gas lanterns, soaked with thorium oxide, glows with a white light far brighter than the flame alone. Thorium is also studied as a fuel for future nuclear reactors.
At night, at a campsite, a gas lantern stands on a tree stump. Its little mantle glows white and lights up the tent and the fir trees around it; the light breathes gently, and moths circle the glass.
Mars rover
A block of plutonium 238 stays hot for decades. Its heat is turned into electricity for Mars rovers and distant space probes, where sunlight is too weak or too dusty.

A rover drives across the rusty plain of Mars under a caramel sky. Its six wheels turn, rocks slide past, and its camera looks around. At the back, the finned plutonium battery glows with warmth, while a dust devil drifts in the distance.
Smoke detector
Most smoke detectors hold a tiny speck of americium. Its rays make the air inside slightly conductive; when smoke gets in, the small current drops and the alarm goes off.

In a kitchen, a burnt slice of toast pops out of the toaster and smoke rises to the ceiling. The detector starts flashing red and ringing. In the magnifying glass, the inside of the detector: the americium speck shoots tiny particles that make charged bits of air move, until the grey smoke gets in their way.
Einstein at the blackboard
Einsteinium was named after Albert Einstein. It was found in 1952 in the debris of the first hydrogen bomb test, and only tiny amounts have ever been made.
Einstein, with his white mane and moustache, writes E = mc² in chalk, walking along the blackboard. He steps back to look at it, then wipes it away with the eraser and starts again.
The periodic table
Mendelevium was named after Dmitri Mendeleev, who arranged the elements in the periodic table in 1869, leaving gaps for elements nobody had found yet.

A periodic table hangs on a classroom wall, its boxes coloured by family. A light runs from box to box, from hydrogen all the way to mendelevium, number 101. Its box lights up in gold, and the teacher\'s pointer taps it twice.
